title: Policy and Legislative Handbook
edition: Second edition · November 2026 · Companion to World Bible v3.4
issuedBy: The Light of Other Stars (public companion)
sourceRef: Policy and Legislative Handbook, second edition; expanded from the Policy and Legislative Ideas Guide
summary: A practical handbook for turning political goals into legislation: resource allocation, fundamental rights, AI government, settlement law and the institutions of a post-superintelligence society. Entries are proposals for debate, not enacted law or new institutional powers.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
paragraphs: This handbook offers competing proposals, legislative instruments and possible bargains. It is not a party manifesto or a prescribed progression. The Assembly governs the release and use of defined extrasolar resource claims. It does not possess general authority over Earth's governments, the domestic economy, or the security system established by the Grand Bargain.

A policy can matter to Assembly politics even when the Assembly cannot enact it alone. National sovereignty, world federation, family life and the authority of security systems shape how people judge the treaty order. Each proposal must identify the part within Assembly jurisdiction and the outside agreement needed for the rest.

Where a legal route is uncertain, consult the [[INST-ARBITER|Office of the Treaty Arbiter]] and, if disputed, the [[INST-TRIBUNAL|Charter Review Tribunal]]. The World Bible and controlling treaty text prevail over shorthand in this handbook. No proposal below establishes a new right, prohibition, office, technology or enforcement mandate merely by appearing here.

sections.heading: Start with the actual decision
list: *What resource claim or treaty rule would change?* Define a release percentage, a channel share, a project, a prohibition, a franchise amendment, or a charter procedure.
*Who receives authority or a claim?* Name beneficiaries, custodians, deadlines and obligations, rather than just an abstract objective.
*Who is protected, and who may intervene?* Define the affected persons, the prohibited conduct, the responsible operator and the limits of any coercive power.
*How can a decision be challenged?* State the evidence standard, review body, emergency time limit and remedy for a wrongful intervention.
*What is the strongest objection?* Identify affected people, future generations, digital minds, existing claimants or preservation interests.
*What is the legal route?* Ordinary vote, enhanced threshold, Council delay or entrenched veto, Tribunal review, or action beyond Assembly jurisdiction.
*What happens ten years later?* Give the World Engine measurable consequences and unresolved risks without prescribing the election result.

*What makes the proposal implementable?* Identify the required technology, deployment stage, resource cost and communication delay; do not assume an overseer is omniscient or physically present everywhere.

sections.heading: Choose a lawful instrument
paragraphs: Different parts of one political programme may require different instruments. Funding a service, prohibiting a use and changing the constitution are separate decisions; one vote does not automatically accomplish all three.

Project conditions apply to prospective treaty-funded activities within the relevant allocation. They must not be used to evade the threshold for a new prohibition, confiscate vested rights or acquire powers outside the treaty. Constitutional recognition of a right may also require a separately classified prohibition or enforcement measure.

sections.heading: Fundamental rights and personal security
paragraphs: The [[DOC-CHARTER|Interim Charter]] already prohibits torture of conscious beings, including digital minds and animals likely to suffer. It does not expressly set out a general protection against killing or deletion. This omission does not repeal domestic criminal law; it leaves a constitutional question about protection across treaty-financed settlements and computing habitats.

Specify the protected subject and the act. Biological death, destruction of a running mind, deletion of a backup, forced suspension and irreversible personality change need not be legally identical. A surviving copy must not automatically be treated as consent to destroy another individual.

sections.heading: Justice, policing and enforcement
paragraphs: Distinguish preventing immediate harm, investigating an alleged offence, deciding liability and imposing a remedy. An AI's technical ability to restrain someone does not settle who authorised it, what evidence is required or how long restraint may last.

The treaty protects Council review of enforcement under Assembly command. An independent verifier, a project operator and a police authority have different mandates even if all use artificial intelligence.

sections.heading: Mental autonomy, persuasion and information
paragraphs: Powerful personal representatives and adaptive environments make influence a matter of institutional design. A person may request help changing their preferences without authorising a sponsor, employer or government to change those preferences secretly.

Rules should distinguish factual correction, disclosed advocacy, voluntary self-transformation and coercive manipulation. They should also protect dissent from the judgement of an allegedly benevolent system.

paragraphs: Abundance of ordinary goods does not remove scarcity of particular locations, trusted institutions, computing capacity or control over infrastructure. An equal initial share of the cosmic pool does not guarantee equal bargaining power indefinitely.

The Assembly may attach lawful prospective conditions to its own allocations and fund alternatives. General Earth-wide competition, taxation or labour law requires the competent outside authorities; vested claims retain their existing protections.

sections.heading: Interstellar public law and security
paragraphs: A title, a launched mission, an inhabited settlement and a functioning local government are different legal facts. Communication delays mean that a rule requiring immediate approval from Earth may be physically impossible to administer.
Defence and enforcement proposals must respect the Grand Bargain and the Council's protected matters. Neither a settlement allocation nor a safety budget silently authorises an armed force.

sections.heading: Welfare across species and artificial worlds
paragraphs: A project can affect animals, artificial minds and unfamiliar forms of life that have no recognised political representative. Uncertainty about consciousness is a reason to specify precaution and evidence standards, not to assert that a preferred theory has been proved.
The existing torture prohibition remains applicable. New welfare duties or bans must identify their legal route and distinguish protection of individual beings from preservation of an ecosystem.

sections.heading: Worked example: preventing violence without creating a machine sovereign
paragraphs: Suppose a coalition proposes an AI safety service for a future Assembly-funded habitat. Distributed robotics or utility fog might be considered only if the required capabilities have been demonstrated and deployment authorised. This example does not establish that such a system exists, is universal or can reliably prevent every harm.

The coalition wants protection against killing and torture. A competing coalition accepts immediate protection but rejects continuous mental surveillance and unreviewable restraint. A third prefers a stronger local enforcer in exchange for security. These are disagreements about rights and governing authority, not merely a choice of equipment.
list: Define the rights and the acts. Identify protected persons and distinguish imminent violence, accidents, consensual activities and contested end-of-life decisions. The torture ban is already law; a new killing or deletion prohibition requires its own legal route.

Define the mandate. State the physical area, operator, permissible interventions and limits on observation. Authority to interrupt immediate harm does not automatically authorise investigation, punishment or a change in someone's mind.
Demonstrate the capability. Publish an independently reviewed safety case, realistic failure modes and resource requirements. Specify what protection remains available during outages or disputes.

Provide immediate and subsequent review. Emergency protection needs a short review clock, accessible representation, independent evidence and a remedy for error. Loss of communications must not make indefinite restraint the default.

Separate the instruments. A project allocation can fund a service; a new prohibition follows the ninety-per-cent route; constitutional changes follow the applicable amendment rules; enforcement under Assembly command faces the Council's protected veto.

Make community choice meaningful. Residents need clear terms and a practical route to challenge or leave an arrangement. A founding operator cannot assume that children or future arrivals have consented merely because the original settlers did.

Specify failure and succession. Identify the responsible institution, compensation fund, replacement process and continuity of essential services. Removing an operator must not itself endanger dependent residents.

Autonomy with minimal coercion

The costs of a harmful act may fall on people who never consented to that risk.

sections.heading: Sovereignty, federalism and political identity
paragraphs: People judge the treaty order through commitments that extend beyond resource allocation. These political currents can run across all six voter families: a nationalist can favour common infrastructure, a federalist can defend individual ownership, and either can support digital welfare.

The positions below are possible organising currents, not additional official voter groups, established organisations or announced changes to the electorate. They suggest political arguments and coalitions that a campaign may develop.

An Assembly campaign may argue for a wider constitutional settlement without claiming that the Assembly can enact world government by an ordinary resource vote. Distinguish a treaty-scope amendment or allocation from a proposal requiring national consent or a new international agreement.

table.caption: Political currents across the voter families
rows: National sovereigntists
Political authority should remain accountable to national communities.
Protect national consent, existing treaty limits and safeguards against domination by larger powers.
Limited international cooperation versus withdrawal; national autonomy versus minority self-government.
World federalists
Common problems warrant a democratic federal constitutional order.
Use treaty reform to strengthen accountable common institutions while specifying reserved national and local powers.
Incremental federation versus a new founding settlement; central capacity versus subsidiarity.
Treaty internationalists
Binding cooperation between continuing sovereign states.
Defend a strong, limited WAER and negotiated agreements without turning it into a general world state.
Equal standing for states versus representation by population; effectiveness versus consent.
Regional integrationists
Regional federations or unions can mediate between nations and the world.
Seek regional participation and balanced access to common programmes.
Regional autonomy versus internal centralisation; representation of people versus governments.
Local and settlement autonomists
Municipalities, communities and distant settlements should govern their own affairs.
Support self-government, practical exit and narrow, specified common obligations.
Resident democracy versus founding property rights; voluntary association versus inherited dependency.
Cosmopolitan egalitarians
Persons' interests should not depend on birthplace or citizenship.
Prioritise equal access, minimum protections and fair distribution across regions.
Equal resources versus equal opportunity or welfare; universal duties versus local democratic choice.
Religious and cultural pluralists
Communities should be able to preserve or develop distinctive ways of life.
Seek voluntary community arrangements, freedom of conscience and protection from forced assimilation.
Collective continuity versus individual dissent; parental authority versus children's future autonomy.
Democratic humanists and machine constitutionalists
The legitimacy and limits of delegated artificial authority.
Humanists emphasise elected control; machine constitutionalists seek binding mandates, review and constraints for delegated systems.
Human final judgement versus bounded AI discretion; democratic choice versus protected individual rights.

sections.heading: Six sample legislative packages
list: *The first-release grand bargain.* A middle-sized release pairs individual endowments with a publicly funded survey network, a future-generation reserve and a narrowly defined AI inquiry allocation. Trade-off: many stakeholders gain a foothold, each receiving less than it might prefer.

*Preservation for participation.* A sanctuary designation combined with a limited settlement franchise and public scientific access. Trade-off: settlers secure a pathway to action while conservation advocates accept some development.

*The constitutional bridge.* A permanent-charter proposal clarifying expiry procedures, Tribunal review, delegation limits and the franchise process without pre-deciding digital enfranchisement. Trade-off: preserves disagreement while making institutions workable.

*Rights with remedies.* Pair defined personal protections with a narrow enforcement mandate, independent review, accessible representation and compensation. Funding and legal authority must be approved through their respective routes. Trade-off: stronger safeguards increase cost and can slow intervention; broad preventive powers increase the risk of domination.

*The autonomous settlement compact.* Combine a resource allocation, prospective local-government terms, a rights floor, migration support and generational revision. Trade-off: settlers gain room to build distinctive institutions while accepting duties to minorities, later residents and outsiders.

*The continuity and open-access bargain.* Pair shared computing and transport infrastructure with portable services, dependent-person continuity reserves and fair access for smaller operators. Trade-off: stronger security and access obligations require resources and limit an operator's commercial discretion.

sections.heading: Using the handbook in a campaign
paragraphs: Choose a goal that reflects your party's priorities; identify a second group that might support it for different reasons; draft the least ambitious instrument that accomplishes the actual objective; and write down the legal uncertainty. A bill that cannot be implemented is not automatically a useful dramatic gesture.

This handbook contains competing proposals, not predictions or enacted decisions. Whether a policy succeeds depends on its legal authority, enacted text, demonstrated capabilities, the scenario state and the transparent adjudication process described in the Operations Manual.
